newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU currency grid to bridge gap for "ins", "outs".
newsitem.headline: EU currency grid to bridge gap for "ins", "outs".

text.p: European Union finance ministers have built their first bridge designed to link those in monetary union and those waiting to join by agreeing the structure of a new currency grid after the launch of the euro.

Officials said the new exchange rate mechanism, the ERM II, whose broad outlines were agreed by finance ministers on Saturday, would help prevent non-members from drifting away from the euro zone when the single currency is launched in 1999.
"The final aim is to have all countries join the euro," French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters after an informal meeting here of finance ministers and central bankers.
"It is in the interests of all for as many as possible to participate," Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said.

Ministers agreed the new ERM II will be based on the current system where currencies are allowed to fluctuate a wide 15 percent either side of a central rate rather than a tight grid abandoned after a currency crisis in 1993.
In the new system, for which final details are meant to be ironed out for approval by EU leaders at a summit in Dublin in December, currencies will be fixed against the euro.

The new currency grid is considered essential to maintain some kind of cohesion in the EU after the single currency is launched, amid worries of a divide between rich northern European countries likely to join first and any countries with weaker economies on the periphery waiting to join.

Officials stressed that though the bands in the new mechanism would be wide enough to give a lot of leeway, ministers were looking at ways of giving it some bite by linking membership to respect for sound monetary and fiscal policies.
"There may be an implicit deal between respect of economic programmes in the (convergence) plan and membership of the ERM II," a Commission spokesman said.
That could mean that the future European Central Bank (ECB) might either stop intervening to support a currency on foreign exchange markets or suggest a devaluation.

"The ECB should have at its discretion the right to suspend intervention if it appers that the amount of intervention would put at risk price stability in the euro area," European Monetary Institute head Alexandre Lamfalussy told reporters.
Procedures are to be improved and speeded up for tracking how well countries waiting to join monetary union are bringing their economies into line with those in the euro zone.
"We emphasised the extent to which multilateral surveillance must be reinforced," Arthuis said.

These plans, if successful, would give non-members which missed the Maastricht treaty standards in 1997 a clear goal to aim for and allow them to sell to their national parliaments the need to keep cutting public spending to reduce budget deficits.
Some key questions on exactly how the ERM II will function will now have to be worked out by EU monetary officials.
Ministers declined to specify a precise figure for the fluctuation bands in the ERM II.

One delegation source said ministers had been asked whether they had any objection to maintaining the current system after the launch of the euro, and none had objected. "My reading of that is that it will be plus or minus 15 percent," he said.

But officials will have to look at how to deal with the unlikely possibility that currencies swing 60 percent against each other -- which could only happen if one started at the maximum 15 percent above the euro and the other 15 percent below, and then reversed positions.
A European Commission spokesman also said that narrower bands were possible for countries with stronger economies, though details on this too have yet to be worked out.
Another key question is over the exact role of the ECB in initiating currency realignments and over how much it will have to take account of the views of the country concerned.
